Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin
A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
Any form of physical contact with others

Threat.value: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

Negative Appraisals.value: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
I am permanently an outsider now

issues.item: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: The social avoidance items are difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. These triggers imply avoidance of people linked to a discrete later-life event, but the trauma is chronic/developmental and caregiver-based; there is no corresponding trigger or appraisal content tying prior social contacts or specific intimacy-linked reminders to the abuse history.

issues.item: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
issues.explanation: Intrusion Monitoring suggests fear of an intruder entering the home, which fits home-invasion or stalking trauma better than childhood caregiver physical abuse. With no accompanying memory or trigger content about nighttime entry, footsteps, doors, or home intrusion, this threat item is hard to explain from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: No Good Ahead and Outsider are broad, depressive or social-identity appraisals, whereas the other active content is dominated by vigilance, bodily threat detection, and sensory triggering. This combination is not impossible, but here the intimacy/social avoidance items appear to depend on relational shame or alienation that is otherwise underdeveloped and weakly connected to the trigger/threat pattern, reducing coherence.

issues.item: No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore
issues.explanation: Given the formulation, Triggers and Negative Appraisals should be tightly linked, but the chosen triggers are mainly tactile/somatic/intrusive-memory cues while two maladaptive strategies focus on avoiding social contacts and intimacy. Those strategies are not well supported by the trigger set and feel targeted at a different symptom cluster than the one represented elsewhere.

vignette:
Arthur presents as a man who has spent a lifetime building walls. At sixty-six, he has a successful career as a software engineer, a long-standing marriage, and a quiet, orderly life that he has meticulously constructed to keep the past at bay. For over fifty years, he has managed the echoes of his childhood, but now, the echoes have become too loud to ignore. The trauma dates back to when he was seven, living with his uncle for a year. The punishments for minor infractions were severe and unpredictable. The memory that surfaces most often, unbidden and sharp, is of being locked in the basement. He can still feel the specific, damp cold of the concrete floor seeping through his thin pyjamas, a chill that has nothing to do with the ambient temperature. He remembers the frantic, rabbit-like thumping of his own heart against his ribs, a sound that seemed to fill the darkness as he waited, certain he would be forgotten there forever.

This history has left indelible marks on his sensory world. A draft from an overzealous office air conditioner can be enough to trigger it; the specific temperature on his skin catapults him back to that basement floor, and for a moment, he is seven years old again, helpless and terrified. Similarly, the normal sensation of his heart racing—whether from climbing a flight of stairs too quickly or the stress of a looming project deadline—is no longer a simple physiological response. For Arthur, the pounding in his chest is a direct line to that childhood terror, a signal that something dreadful is about to happen. His body seems to hold the memory more viscerally than his mind, reacting to perceived danger before he has even had time to consciously register a threat.

Over the decades, Arthur has learned to navigate a world he perceives as fundamentally unsafe. He has come to believe that constant vigilance is the only rational way to live, because you truly never know what can happen next. When entering any room, his eyes perform an unconscious, sweeping inventory of potential dangers, clocking heavy objects, sharp corners, or anything that could conceivably be used as a weapon. This internal threat assessment is as automatic to him as breathing. It has fostered a deep and abiding mistrust of others. He is certain that people, even those with good intentions, are ultimately unreliable and capable of causing harm. This conviction has made him feel like a permanent outsider, observing the easy camaraderie of his colleagues or the casual affection between other couples from behind an invisible barrier.

To manage this constant sense of threat, Arthur has systematically narrowed his life. Physical contact is the most difficult. An unexpected hand on his shoulder from a colleague can cause him to flinch with an alarm that is startling to everyone involved. He has learned to position himself in meetings to avoid anyone getting behind him. At home, he avoids being touched by his wife, a pattern that has, over many years, eroded the physical intimacy between them. What she sees as rejection, he experiences as a necessary act of self-preservation. He has also gradually withdrawn from social life. The team lunches and after-work drinks he used to attend became too fraught with the potential for unpredictable interactions, so he started making excuses. Now, he socialises with almost no one he knew before the event became so acute in his mind. He even finds himself avoiding his own reflection, averting his gaze from his own body, as if it is a separate entity that holds all the pain and fear he cannot bear to confront.

It was his wife, after another pained and disconnected evening, who finally gave him an ultimatum. Her tears, and her words about feeling married to a ghost, broke through the fortress he had built. Arthur is now seeking help, not with any grand hope of transformation, but with the quiet, desperate wish that he might be able to feel safe in his own skin, in his own home, for the first time in his life. He is terrified of dredging up the past, but what frightens him more is the prospect of living out the rest of his years as a stranger to the person who loves him most.
